title: Image compression
text:
Entropy coding started in the late 1940s with the introduction of Shannon–Fano coding,[1] the basis for Huffman coding which was published in 1952.[2] Transform coding dates back to the late 1960s, with the introduction of fast Fourier transform (FFT) coding in 1968 and the Hadamard transform in 1969.[3]

An important development in image data compression was the discrete cosine transform (DCT), a lossy compression technique first proposed by Nasir Ahmed, T. Natarajan and K. R. Rao in 1973.[4] JPEG was introduced by the Joint Photographic Experts Group (JPEG) in 1992.[5] JPEG compresses images down to much smaller file sizes, and has become the most widely used image file format.[6] JPEG was largely responsible for the wide proliferation of digital images and digital photos,[7] with several billion JPEG images produced every day as of 2015.[8]

Lempel–Ziv–Welch (LZW) is a lossless compression algorithm developed by Abraham Lempel, Jacob Ziv and Terry Welch in 1984. It is used in the GIF format, introduced in 1987.[9] DEFLATE, a lossless compression algorithm developed by Phil Katz and specified in 1996, is used in the Portable Network Graphics (PNG) format.[10]

The JPEG 2000 standard was developed from 1997 to 2000 by a JPEG committee chaired by Touradj Ebrahimi (later the JPEG president).[11] In contrast to the DCT algorithm used by the original JPEG format, JPEG 2000 instead uses discrete wavelet transform (DWT) algorithms. It uses the CDF 9/7 wavelet transform (developed by Ingrid Daubechies in 1992) for its lossy compression algorithm,[12] and the Le Gall–Tabatabai (LGT) 5/3 wavelet transform[13,14] (developed by Didier Le Gall and Ali J. Tabatabai in 1988)[15] for its lossless compression algorithm.[12] JPEG 2000 technology, which includes the Motion JPEG 2000 extension, was selected as the video coding standard for digital cinema in 2004.[16]
